title: Treasury Cancels Booz Allen Contracts After IRS Data Leak
description_short: Treasury canceled 31 Booz Allen contracts after an IRS contractor leaked taxpayer records; the department cited data safeguards and vetting.
description_medium: On January 26, 2026, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced cancellation of all 31 department contracts with Booz Allen Hamilton, totaling $21 million in obligations. Treasury cited inadequate safeguards for sensitive taxpayer data and the prior theft and disclosure of records by former Booz Allen employee Charles Littlejohn. Bessent later told senators that Treasury had lost confidence in the firm’s vetting of contractors. The sources do not show the decision was made to protect Bessent, Trump, or other wealthy taxpayers.
description_long: The Treasury Department announced on January 26, 2026, that it was canceling all 31 of its contracts with Booz Allen Hamilton. The department said the contracts represented $4.8 million in annual spending and $21 million in total obligations. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the firm had failed to provide adequate safeguards for sensitive taxpayer information available through its IRS contracts. The department cited Charles Edward Littlejohn, a former Booz Allen employee who stole and disclosed tax information between 2018 and 2020; Treasury said the breach affected about 406,000 taxpayers. The Associated Press reported the cancellations and the prior criminal case. In April, Bessent told senators that Treasury had lost confidence in Booz Allen’s screening and vetting of contractors, and the company noted the employee used government systems. This evidence supports reporting the cancellation and the government’s stated reasons. It does not establish that Bessent acted to shield himself, Trump, or billionaires named in news coverage of the leak. Nor does it show that canceling the contracts altered anyone’s tax liability. The original motive claim and environmental classification should be removed.
notes: Treasury’s January 26, 2026 release confirms the contract count, amounts, and its stated data-safeguard rationale. AP reports the underlying Littlejohn case. FedScoop reports Bessent’s April congressional explanation centered on contractor vetting. No source establishes the asserted personal-protection motive.
proposed_correction: Treasury canceled 31 Booz Allen contracts following the IRS data leak, citing safeguards and contractor vetting; a motive to protect Bessent, Trump, or billionaires is unsupported.

sources.what_it_supports: Treasury’s statement on canceling 31 Booz Allen contracts, amounts, and stated data-safeguard rationale.
AP report on contract cancellations and the underlying Littlejohn IRS-data case.
Bessent’s April congressional explanation focused on contractor screening and vetting.

supported_facts: Treasury announced cancellation of all 31 Booz Allen contracts on January 26, 2026.
The contracts totaled $4.8 million in annual spending and $21 million in total obligations.
Treasury linked the action to taxpayer-data safeguards and the Littlejohn leak; it said the breach affected about 406,000 taxpayers.
Bessent told senators that Treasury no longer had confidence in the firm’s screening and vetting of contractors.
limitations: No decision record or independent reporting establishes a motive to protect Bessent, Trump, or wealthy taxpayers.
The contract action does not establish any change in the tax obligations of people whose records were leaked.
The old environmental category does not fit the supported event.
evidence_resolution.proposed_title: Treasury Cancels Booz Allen Contracts After IRS Data Leak
evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: Treasury canceled 31 Booz Allen contracts following the IRS data leak, citing safeguards and contractor vetting; a motive to protect Bessent, Trump, or billionaires is unsupported.

title: Federal Courts Block USCIS Holds Affecting Applications from 39 Countries
description_short: USCIS placed immigration applications on hold for people from 39 countries; courts later ordered the challenged policies vacated.
description_medium: USCIS memoranda issued in December 2025 and January 2026 directed holds on certain pending benefit applications, expanding the policy to nationals of 39 countries. In April, a Massachusetts judge ordered preliminary relief for 22 plaintiffs who showed harm. A Rhode Island court later vacated the challenged hold policies, and final judgment entered June 11, 2026; USCIS said the vacatur applied agency-wide. The supplied AP report covers that later ruling, not a universal six-month freeze.
description_long: USCIS issued Policy Memorandum 602-0192 in December 2025 and 602-0194 in January 2026. The later memorandum extended an adjudicative hold to applicants from the 39 countries listed in the relevant travel proclamation, subject to stated exceptions. In an April 30, 2026 case in Massachusetts, Judge Julia Kobick granted preliminary relief to plaintiffs who demonstrated concrete harm; the order initially covered 22 plaintiffs in that case, not every applicant from the 39 countries. Separately, on June 5, 2026, a Rhode Island federal court vacated the challenged USCIS hold policies. Final judgment entered June 11. USCIS’s own notice says that vacatur applied agency-wide and that the memoranda should be treated as not in effect, while noting that the agency disagreed and might seek further review. The Associated Press reported the June ruling and described the affected application types, including asylum, work permits, green cards, and citizenship applications. The evidence supports a bounded account of the hold and subsequent court action. It does not support the preserved claim that every application was frozen for six months or that April relief applied universally.
organization_tags: U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island

preserved_fields.title: USCIS Illegally Freezes All Immigration Benefits for 39-Country Nationals for Six Months
preserved_fields.description_short: USCIS Illegally Freezes All Immigration Benefits for 39-Country Nationals for Six Months
preserved_fields.description_medium: Beginning in December 2025, USCIS Policy Memorandum 602-0192 placed an indefinite hold on all pending immigration benefit applications, asylum, green cards, work permits, naturalization, filed by nationals of 39 countries, leaving thousands of lawful applicants in legal limbo for up to six months. A Boston federal court found in April 2026 that the adjudicative hold violated the Administrative Procedure Act, was applied without notice-and-comment rulemaking, and likely violated Fifth Amendment due process and equal protection rights. The administration argued courts lacked jurisdiction.

notes: USCIS policy memoranda and the April 30 Massachusetts order establish the hold and limited preliminary relief. AP reports the June 5 Rhode Island ruling. USCIS confirms that June 11 final judgment vacated the policies agency-wide. The sources refute the earlier universal six-month description.
proposed_correction: USCIS imposed holds on certain pending applications from nationals of 39 countries, then federal courts granted limited preliminary relief and later vacated the challenged hold policies agency-wide.

sources.what_it_supports: AP report on the June 2026 ruling affecting USCIS policies and applicants from 39 countries.
Massachusetts court’s April 30 opinion on the holds and scope of preliminary relief.
USCIS notice that the Rhode Island court’s June 2026 vacatur applied agency-wide.
USCIS January 1, 2026 memorandum extending the hold to nationals of additional high-risk countries.

supported_facts: USCIS issued PM 602-0192 on December 2, 2025 and PM 602-0194 on January 1, 2026.
PM 602-0194 extended the adjudicative hold to nationals of 39 countries, with exceptions.
The April 30 Massachusetts preliminary order initially covered 22 plaintiffs who demonstrated harm.
A Rhode Island court vacated the hold policies on June 5; final judgment entered June 11, and USCIS said the vacatur applied agency-wide.
limitations: The April preliminary order did not automatically cover all 39-country applicants.
The supplied AP story is about the later June court ruling; separate court and agency records establish the policy details and final scope.
The record does not support a universal six-month freeze.
evidence_resolution.proposed_title: Federal Courts Block USCIS Holds Affecting Applications from 39 Countries
evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: USCIS imposed holds on certain pending applications from nationals of 39 countries, then federal courts granted limited preliminary relief and later vacated the challenged hold policies agency-wide.

title: Trump University Manager Describes Pressure on Financially Struggling Students
description_short: A former Trump University sales manager said staff pushed financially struggling students toward costly real-estate courses.
description_medium: In a sworn declaration filed in Trump University litigation, former sales manager Ronald Schnackenberg said he was reprimanded after declining to push a financially struggling couple toward a $35,000 course. He also said speakers urged students to raise credit-card limits to buy higher-priced courses. The New York Times reported the declaration in 2016. These are attributed allegations and testimony, not findings made in the cited materials.
description_long: Ronald Schnackenberg, a former Trump University sales manager, described the school’s sales practices in a sworn declaration filed in litigation. He said that speakers told students to seek higher credit-card limits so they could buy real-estate courses, including the next level of Trump University programs. Schnackenberg also recounted being reprimanded after he declined to press a financially struggling couple to enroll in a $35,000 course because he believed it would endanger their finances; he said another salesperson persuaded them to buy it. The New York Times reported on the declaration when the documents were unsealed in June 2016. The account supports a carefully attributed description of the alleged sales pressure and the specific example in Schnackenberg’s statement. It does not by itself establish every practice at the school, a quantified range of student losses, or a judicial finding that all students were targeted because they were elderly or vulnerable. The supplied New York Times link is an unrelated 2006 opinion piece and cannot substantiate the later litigation. The direct declaration and contemporaneous 2016 reporting are the appropriate evidence for this narrower entry.
notes: The linked 2006 NYT opinion predates these events. The sworn Schnackenberg declaration and 2016 NYT report support the attributed account of pressure to raise credit limits and the $35,000 course example; they do not establish a broad quantified loss range or a judicial finding.
proposed_correction: A sworn declaration by former Trump University sales manager Ronald Schnackenberg described pressure to increase credit limits and a $35,000 course sale to a financially struggling couple.

sources.what_it_supports: Sworn declaration by former Trump University sales manager Ronald Schnackenberg.
2016 NYT reporting on the unsealed Schnackenberg declaration.

supported_facts: Schnackenberg said he worked as a Trump University sales manager in 2006–2007.
His declaration says speakers urged students to raise credit-card limits to purchase further courses.
He said he was reprimanded after declining to sell a $35,000 course to a financially struggling couple; he said another salesperson sold it.
The New York Times reported on the unsealed declaration in June 2016.
limitations: These are claims in a sworn declaration, reported as litigation evidence; this summary does not treat them as a court finding.
The supplied 2006 NYT opinion predates the declaration and does not support these facts.
The packet’s $5,000–$35,000 student-loss range and broader claims about instructor evaluations are not established by these sources.
evidence_resolution.proposed_title: Trump University Manager Describes Pressure on Financially Struggling Students
evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: A sworn declaration by former Trump University sales manager Ronald Schnackenberg described pressure to increase credit limits and a $35,000 course sale to a financially struggling couple.

title: Rudy Giuliani Holds Election-Fraud Press Conference at Four Seasons Total Landscaping
description_short: Giuliani alleged widespread fraud at a November 7, 2020 press conference outside Four Seasons Total Landscaping in Philadelphia.
description_medium: On November 7, 2020, Rudy Giuliani held a press conference in the parking lot of Four Seasons Total Landscaping in Philadelphia and alleged widespread voter fraud while challenging the election result for Donald Trump. The Associated Press reported that courts had found no evidence supporting the campaign’s broad fraud claims. The Philadelphia Inquirer said Giuliani alleged misconduct without presenting evidence and that Trump had announced the venue as “Four Seasons, Philadelphia,” prompting confusion with the hotel.
description_long: Rudy Giuliani, then Donald Trump’s personal lawyer, held a press conference on November 7, 2020, in the parking lot of Four Seasons Total Landscaping in Philadelphia. The event was part of the Trump campaign’s effort to challenge the 2020 election result. Giuliani alleged widespread voter fraud and said the campaign would bring legal action. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that he accused city election administrators of submitting ballots and accepting ballots cast in the names of dead people without presenting evidence at the event. The Inquirer also reported that Trump’s announcement had referred to “Four Seasons, Philadelphia,” which led some to expect the Four Seasons Hotel; the actual event took place at the landscaping business in Northeast Philadelphia. The Associated Press later described the press conference as part of a legal effort whose broad fraud claims were not supported by court findings. This evidence supports the location, date, speaker, and nature of the allegations, provided the allegations remain attributed to Giuliani and are not presented as established facts. The original AP link in the row concerns Trump’s call to Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, not this press conference, so event-specific reporting has been added.

title: Kushner Used WhatsApp for Official White House Business, Including with Foreign Contacts
description_short: Kushner’s lawyer told lawmakers he used WhatsApp for official business and sent message screenshots to official accounts for preservation.
description_medium: In March 2019, House Oversight Chairman Elijah Cummings said Jared Kushner’s lawyer had confirmed Kushner used WhatsApp for official White House business, including with foreign contacts. The lawyer said Kushner took screenshots and sent them to his White House email or the National Security Council. He could not say whether any messages contained classified information. This documents the reported app use and preservation method, not a proven records violation or security breach.
description_long: In March 2019, House Oversight Chairman Elijah Cummings wrote to the White House about Jared Kushner’s use of private messaging services. Cummings said Kushner’s lawyer had told lawmakers that Kushner used WhatsApp for official White House business, including communications with foreign contacts. The lawyer said Kushner took screenshots of the messages and sent them to his official White House email account or the National Security Council, and asserted that this complied with records requirements. The New York Times and ABC News reported Cummings’s account of the lawyer’s statements. The lawyer could not say whether Kushner had used WhatsApp to transmit classified information. The reporting therefore supports the fact that the app was used for official business and describes the stated preservation method. It does not establish that the messages were lost, unpreserved, classified, or involved a security breach. A separate CNN report cited in the coverage concerned communications with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, but the supplied record does not provide message content or dates. The entry should focus on the reported official use of WhatsApp and keep both the preservation claim and the uncertainty about message contents attributed to counsel and lawmakers.
organization_tags: House Committee on Oversight and Reform
notes: The linked NYT report is accessible through Exa and covers the March 2019 committee disclosure. Cummings’s description of counsel’s account says screenshots were forwarded to official accounts. Counsel claimed compliance; the available sources do not establish loss of records, classified content, or a security breach.
proposed_correction: Kushner used WhatsApp for official White House business, including foreign contacts; his counsel said he forwarded screenshots to official accounts and could not confirm whether any messages were classified.

sources.what_it_supports: NYT account of House Oversight’s disclosure about WhatsApp use and the lawyer’s preservation explanation.
ABC report on the committee letter, foreign contacts, and screenshot forwarding account.
Politico account of Cummings’s report and counsel’s record-preservation claim.

supported_facts: Cummings reported in March 2019 that Kushner’s lawyer acknowledged official-business use of WhatsApp, including with foreign contacts.
Counsel said Kushner sent screenshots to his White House account or the NSC.
Counsel could not say whether the communications included classified information.
limitations: The sources do not establish that messages were unpreserved or deleted.
The claim of legal compliance is counsel’s statement, not a committee finding.
No message text or precise communication dates are supplied; the evidence does not establish classified disclosure or security exposure.
evidence_resolution.proposed_title: Kushner Used WhatsApp for Official White House Business, Including with Foreign Contacts
evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: Kushner used WhatsApp for official White House business, including foreign contacts; his counsel said he forwarded screenshots to official accounts and could not confirm whether any messages were classified.

title: Trump Grants Full Pardon to Dinesh D’Souza After Campaign-Finance Conviction
description_short: Trump issued Dinesh D’Souza a full pardon on May 31, 2018, after a campaign-finance conviction and sentence of probation and a fine.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s pardon instrument records a full and unconditional pardon for Dinesh D’Souza, dated May 31, 2018. It identifies his campaign-finance conviction and sentence: five years’ probation, including eight months of community confinement, community service, and a $30,000 fine. The White House said Trump viewed him as a victim of selective prosecution and noted his acceptance of responsibility. The records establish the grant and stated rationale, not that it was corrupt.
description_long: On May 31, 2018, President Donald Trump granted Dinesh D’Souza a full and unconditional pardon. The Justice Department’s published pardon instrument identifies D’Souza’s conviction in the Southern District of New York for campaign-finance violations and records his sentence: five years of probation, including eight months of community confinement, one day per week of community service, and a $30,000 fine. A White House statement said Trump considered D’Souza a victim of selective prosecution. It also said D’Souza accepted responsibility and had completed community service teaching English to people seeking citizenship. The instrument and statement support the date, recipient, conviction category, sentence, and administration’s stated rationale. They do not establish that the pardon was corrupt, that Trump granted it in exchange for something, or that D’Souza had been deprived of lawful process. The supplied Justice Department index and AP topic page were not sufficient to establish those details, so the case-specific pardon instrument and archived White House statement are added. The catalog entry should describe the pardon neutrally and remove the unsupported “Corrupt Pardons” label unless separate evidence establishes an improper exchange or motive.
notes: The case-specific DOJ instrument confirms a full and unconditional pardon and the sentence; the archived White House statement gives the administration’s stated reason. Neither establishes corruption or an exchange.
proposed_correction: Trump granted Dinesh D’Souza a full pardon on May 31, 2018 following a campaign-finance conviction; the White House described its rationale as selective prosecution.

evidence_resolution.proposed_title: Trump Grants Full Pardon to Dinesh D’Souza After Campaign-Finance Conviction
evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: Trump granted Dinesh D’Souza a full pardon on May 31, 2018 following a campaign-finance conviction; the White House described its rationale as selective prosecution.

title: No Verified Trump Commutation for Mathew G. Charles
description_short: The DOJ list has no exact Mathew G. Charles entry; reporting on Matthew Charles describes a court resentencing, not a Trump commutation.
description_medium: The supplied Justice Department list of Trump’s 2017–2021 commutations contains no exact entry for Mathew G. Charles. The similar-name case in NPR reporting concerns Matthew Charles, whose sentence was reduced to time served by a federal judge under the First Step Act in January 2019 after prosecutors did not oppose release. That is a judicial resentencing, not a presidential commutation. The identity and claimed grant remain unresolved.
description_long: The assigned record says President Donald Trump commuted the sentence of “Mathew G. Charles,” but the linked Justice Department list of Trump commutations from 2017 through 2021 contains no exact-name entry. The list cannot establish the claimed grant, the recipient’s identity, the offense, or the terms. A similar-name case in NPR’s January 2019 reporting concerns Matthew Charles, whose sentence was reduced to time served by U.S. District Judge Aleta Trauger under the First Step Act. NPR reported that federal prosecutors did not oppose the request and that a presidential clemency petition had been pending; the release described in the story followed the judge’s ruling, not a Trump commutation. Georgetown Law likewise describes Charles’s release as a lawful resentencing under the statute. The spelling and absence of a middle initial mean these sources do not prove that the assigned “Mathew G. Charles” is the same person. They do, however, show a plausible conflation and provide no support for publishing the presidential-clemency claim. Exclude the claimed commutation unless a matching official clemency instrument or a corrected recipient identity is supplied. Do not substitute the unrelated judicial resentencing as a Trump action.
notes: The official Trump commutations list has no exact “Mathew G. Charles” match. NPR and Georgetown Law describe a different-spelled Matthew Charles as released following a judge’s First Step Act resentencing; they do not document a presidential commutation. Exclude pending a matching clemency instrument or corrected identity.
proposed_correction: No supplied official source verifies a Trump commutation for Mathew G. Charles; the similar Matthew Charles case was a judicial resentencing under the First Step Act.

sources.what_it_supports: Official list of commutations granted during Trump’s first term; no exact Mathew G. Charles entry appears in the reviewed text.
NPR report that Matthew Charles’s release followed judicial resentencing under the First Step Act.
Georgetown Law account describing Matthew Charles’s statutory resentencing, not a presidential commutation.

supported_facts: The linked DOJ Trump commutations list has no exact “Mathew G. Charles” entry.
NPR reports that Matthew Charles was resentenced to time served by a federal judge under the First Step Act on January 3, 2019.
NPR reports prosecutors did not oppose the judicial resentencing and that a clemency petition had been pending.
Georgetown Law also identifies the release as a statutory resentencing, not a presidential commutation.
limitations: The spelling and middle initial differ; available reporting does not prove Matthew Charles and the named “Mathew G. Charles” are the same person.
No case-specific presidential clemency instrument has been identified.
Do not treat the unrelated judicial resentencing as Trump’s act.
evidence_resolution.proposed_title: No Verified Trump Commutation for Mathew G. Charles
evidence_resolution.proposed_claim: No supplied official source verifies a Trump commutation for Mathew G. Charles; the similar Matthew Charles case was a judicial resentencing under the First Step Act.
